topStories.headline: Board Votes to Extend Data Center Ban Another 10 Months — SoMa and Dogpatch Sites Directly in Scope
topStories.dek: San Francisco supervisors voted unanimously on November 17 to freeze new data center construction through September 2027, citing a power grid that is already close to its capacity ceiling.
topStories.body:
The San Francisco Board of Supervisors voted on Tuesday, November 17, to extend the city's moratorium on new data centers by roughly ten and a half months, keeping the freeze in place through September 2027. The original 45-day pause was set to expire at the end of November; Tuesday's vote prevents any new stand-alone facility from breaking ground while city planners complete a fuller study of land-use and environmental impacts.

The vote carries direct consequences for South of Market and Dogpatch. According to SFist, developers have already scouted potential data center projects at the shuttered San Francisco Centre mall downtown as well as sites in both SoMa and Dogpatch. A Planning Department report released ahead of the vote found that the city's power transmission is approaching its 1,000-megawatt ceiling even without any new data center construction — and estimated that a single 50-megawatt facility could consume as much electricity as 25,000 homes.

Supervisor Shamann Walton, who originally sponsored the 45-day pause, also sponsored the extension. The measure was co-sponsored by Supervisors Jackie Fielder, Chyanne Chen, and Connie Chan. It passed without dissent; Supervisor Chan was the only absentee. Under city rules, the extension takes effect in ten days unless Mayor Daniel Lurie returns it, though any veto could be overridden by a four-fifths vote of the board.

The moratorium reflects a broader tension the city is navigating between its ambitions as an AI hub and the hard limits of its electrical infrastructure. Planners are now tasked with answering open questions about whether to cap total data center power consumption, how to update the zoning code, and what to do about diesel backup generators that kick in during outages.

topStories.headline: Mission Bay Neighbors Push Back on Amazon's Delivery Depot, Want Housing Instead
topStories.dek: The Housing Action Coalition and the Mission Bay Neighborhood Association have formally asked the Planning Department to reconsider letting Amazon build a 710,000-square-foot delivery warehouse at 900 Seventh Street.
topStories.body:
A coalition of Mission Bay residents and housing advocates is making a fresh push this month to redirect a full city block near the Caltrain corridor away from Amazon's proposed delivery depot and toward housing. The Housing Action Coalition and the Mission Bay Neighborhood Association asked the San Francisco Planning Department last summer to consider the site at 900 Seventh Street for housing rather than Amazon's planned 710,000-square-foot fulfillment center; their November report in the Potrero View signals that opposition has not faded.

Amazon purchased the six-acre parcel — formerly used as a Recology work yard — in December 2020 for approximately $202 million, putting an end to earlier plans for up to a thousand residential units on the site. The proposed facility, known internally as DOT9, would be three stories tall and dispatch as many as 200 delivery vans into surrounding neighborhoods every day. It has not broken ground, and critics say its location between the emerging Showplace Square district and Mission Bay actively works against the urban fabric the city has spent years trying to stitch together.

The Sierra Club's San Francisco Group also formally opposes the project. Peter Belden, a Potrero Hill resident and the group's political chair, cited concerns about overconsumption, air pollution, and reduced street safety. Planning Department communications director Patrick Hannan noted that before Amazon can obtain a building permit, it will need to demonstrate the facility can handle its expected energy demand — a threshold that may prove more complicated in light of the city's newly extended data center and power-grid concerns.

topStories.headline: Potrero Hill's Jackson Park Gets Its $48 Million Renovation — but the Tennis Court Is Going Away
topStories.dek: The long-planned overhaul of Jackson Playground received a $10 million state grant this fall, locking in construction for late 2027 — and confirming that the park's lone tennis court will not survive the redesign.
topStories.body:
Jackson Playground on Potrero Hill cleared a major funding hurdle this autumn when the state awarded $10 million toward a planned $48 million renovation of the 4.4-acre park. The San Francisco Recreation and Park Department said the grant — which still requires approval from the Board of Supervisors — will help finance new playgrounds, a dedicated dog run, reconfigured ballfields, a community garden, and a new outdoor multi-use court. Construction is expected to begin in late 2027 and finish in 2029.

The project has been a decade in the making, driven by the Friends of Jackson Park and shaped through extensive community input. The redesign will also expand the park's clubhouse by roughly 1,850 square feet, adding a kitchen, restrooms, and a stage to support after-school programs and community events. About $6 million in total funding still needs to be raised.

One element of the plan is drawing pointed concern from regular park users: the renovation will eliminate the park's existing tennis court and replace it with a single backboard as part of the multi-use court. Tennis coach Tommy Purcell, who works at the park, told the Potrero View that the court is heavily used and that combining basketball, futsal, pickleball, climbing, and a tennis wall in one shared space will create competition and conflict. Recreation and Park responded that the decision was not made out of indifference to tennis, and noted that players will need to use other courts in the city once demolition begins. Officials pointed to recent improvements at McLaren Park as one alternative.

moreNews.headline: SF Port Has a New Executive Director — and He Already Calls the City Home
moreNews.body: Michael Martin was appointed Executive Director of the Port of San Francisco in November 2026, according to the Potrero View. Martin, a Boston native and George Washington University Law School graduate, moved to San Francisco in 2000 intending to stay for a year and never left. He spent his career in public sector and municipal development work in the city. The Port oversees the waterfront from Fisherman's Wharf to the southern end of Dogpatch and plays a central role in ongoing development at Pier 70 and the Mission Bay shoreline.

moreNews.headline: Dogpatch Biotech Revel Pharmaceuticals Published Anti-Aging Enzyme Findings in Nature Communications
moreNews.body: Revel Pharmaceuticals, a longevity startup based in Dogpatch, published peer-reviewed findings in Nature Communications in July showing that its engineered enzyme CMLase can reverse a form of protein damage — known as CML glycation — that accumulates in human tissue over decades and was long considered permanent. In tests on preserved arterial and skin samples, the enzyme eliminated more than 70 percent of CML damage in arterial tissue from a 75-year-old donor and reversed markers in aged skin to levels typical of a 31-year-old. The research, conducted with Calico Life Sciences and the University of Colorado, opens potential paths to therapies for inflammatory conditions tied to aging including heart and kidney disease, skin stiffening, and cataracts. The Potrero View covered the breakthrough in its October 2026 issue.
